title: Mapping the z>=5 SiIV Column Density Distribution onto the Galaxy Stellar Mass Function Using the Cumulative Absorption Cross Section
comment: 22 Pages, 14 figures, accepted to ApJ, where the definitive version is available
summary: Efforts to constrain directly the activity in low-mass galaxies confront sensitivity limits even in the JWST era. Metal absorbers offer a complementary probe and are easier to detect, but leveraging them requires a known relationship between absorber strength and host mass. To this end, many studies assume a simple monotonic relationship between absorber strength and host mass. This ansatz ignores evidence that galaxies at fixed luminosity host absorbers spanning a variety of strengths. We address this issue by deriving a six-parameter model for the cumulative absorption cross section from cosmological simulations that combines with the galaxy stellar mass function to predict the absorber column density distribution (CDD). A maximum-likelihood analysis confirms that this approach reconciles the observed galaxy stellar mass function with the observed SiIV CDD at z=5-6. The extrapolated CDD grows uncertain outside the observed range and the resulting constraints contain degeneracies, highlighting the need for improved measurements. Galaxies of all masses host absorbers of all strengths, but a weak empirical association between massive galaxies and strong absorbers is indicated. Faint galaxies (M* < 10^8 Msun) host the majority of weak SiIV absorbers (log N < 13), emphasizing emission/absorber complementarity. The assumption of a power-law relationship between absorbers' geometric cross sections and host galaxy masses is empirically disfavored. The model may be applied to any combination of ion and redshift if the galaxy stellar mass function is well-constrained. Future observational tests incorporating improved host statistics will extend the model's range.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a six-parameter model from cosmological simulations linking cumulative absorption cross sections to galaxy stellar mass functions, predicting the SiIV absorber column density distribution (CDD) at z=5-6. The model reconciles observed galaxy mass functions with observed SiIV CDD, reveals that galaxies of all masses host absorbers of all strengths with a weak massive-galaxy/strong-absorber association, and disfavors a simple power-law relationship between absorber cross sections and host mass. Faint galaxies (M* < 10^8 Msun) dominate weak SiIV absorbers, highlighting emission-absorption complementarity.
AI.motivation: Direct constraints on activity in low-mass galaxies are sensitivity-limited even with JWST, so metal absorbers offer a complementary probe. However, exploiting absorbers requires a known relationship between absorber strength and host mass, and the common assumption of a simple monotonic link ignores evidence that galaxies at fixed luminosity host absorbers of varying strength.
AI.method: A six-parameter model for the cumulative absorption cross section is derived from cosmological simulations and combined with the galaxy stellar mass function to predict the absorber column density distribution (CDD). A maximum-likelihood analysis is used to reconcile observed galaxy stellar mass functions with the observed SiIV CDD at z=5-6.
AI.result: The approach successfully reconciles the observed galaxy stellar mass function with the observed SiIV CDD at z=5-6. Extrapolation outside the observed range is uncertain with degeneracies in constraints. Weak empirical association between massive galaxies and strong absorbers is found, faint galaxies dominate weak SiIV absorbers (log N < 13), and a power-law relationship between absorber geometric cross sections and host galaxy masses is empirically disfavored.
AI.conclusion: Galaxies of all masses host absorbers of all strengths, with emission/absorber complementarity emphasized for faint galaxies. The model generalizes to any ion and redshift where the galaxy stellar mass function is well-constrained, and future observational tests with improved host statistics will extend its range.

title: Pandora cluster Lensing, AGN, and Transient Exploration (PLATE) from JWST Multi-Epoch Imaging. I. Discovery of a type II supernova candidate in a spiral galaxy at $z=0.7$
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, submitted to Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy of Science China
summary: We report the discovery and multi-wavelength analysis of a $z\sim0.7$ transient PLATE-23a in the Abell 2744 field, as the first results of the Pandora Lensing, AGN, and Transient Exploration (PLATE) project. Using multi-epoch JWST NIRCam imaging spanning from 2022 to 2025, we detect PLATE-23a in 12 filters. Difference-imaging analysis reveals its rising and declining phases. The host galaxy of PLATE-23a is a barred spiral at $z=0.688$ with a stellar mass of $\sim 10^{10.4}M_{\odot}$ and a star formation rate of $\sim5.1M_{\odot}~\rm yr^{-1}$, placing it on the star-forming main sequence. Bayesian light-curve classification strongly favors a type IIP supernova (SN) origin. It lies $\sim 13\rm kpc$ (after lensing correction) from the galaxy center in a region of low local star formation, suggesting the progenitor may have migrated from a distant star-forming clump. Physical properties derived from blackbody modeling indicate a temperature decreasing from $\sim8010\rm K$ to $\sim6100\rm K$ at around 65 days after the explosion; the late-time SED is consistent with entering the radioactive decay phase at about one rest-frame year. This work demonstrates the power of deep, multi-epoch JWST observations for studying transients at cosmological distances.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the discovery of PLATE-23a, a z~0.7 type IIP supernova in the Abell 2744 field, detected using multi-epoch JWST NIRCam imaging across 12 filters. The host is a barred spiral galaxy with stellar mass ~10^10.4 M_sun and SFR ~5.1 M_sun/yr. Light-curve classification and blackbody modeling (temperature declining from ~8010K to ~6100K) confirm a type IIP SN origin, and the progenitor likely migrated from a distant star-forming clump. This is the first result from the PLATE (Pandora Lensing, AGN, and Transient Exploration) project.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the capability of deep, multi-epoch JWST observations for discovering and characterizing transients at cosmological distances (z~0.7), and to present the first results from the PLATE project studying supernovae in lensed and deep fields.
AI.method: Multi-epoch JWST NIRCam imaging (2022-2025) with difference-imaging analysis to detect rising and declining phases; Bayesian light-curve classification; blackbody spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling; host galaxy stellar population analysis; lensing corrections applied to determine physical distances.
AI.result: PLATE-23a is detected in 12 filters with clear rising and declining phases. It is classified as a type IIP supernova by Bayesian analysis. The host is a star-forming barred spiral at z=0.688. The SN lies ~13 kpc (lens-corrected) from the galaxy center in a low star formation region. Blackbody temperature decreases from ~8010K to ~6100K at ~65 days post-explosion, with late-time SED consistent with the radioactive decay phase at ~1 rest-frame year.
AI.conclusion: PLATE-23a is a type IIP supernova at z~0.7 whose progenitor likely migrated from a distant star-forming clump. This work highlights the power of deep, multi-epoch JWST observations for studying transients at cosmological distances and serves as a demonstration of the PLATE project's scientific capabilities.

title: Ultra-Deep imaging of the starless galaxy candidate Cloud-9
comment: Accepted for publication in Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society
summary: We report the non-detection of stellar light associated with the dark galaxy candidate Cloud-9. Ultra-deep imaging obtained with HiPERCAM at the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) reaches surface-brightness limits of 31.4 and 31.0 mag/arcsec$^2$ in g and r, respectively, approximately ten times deeper than previous deep imaging of the region. No stellar emission is detected within the central 1'$\times$1' ($\sim$1.3$\times$1.3 kpc) region of Cloud-9. Assuming an old, metal-poor stellar population, these limits imply a stellar surface mass density of no more than $\sim$0.01 M$_\odot$/pc$^2$ and an upper limit on the total stellar mass of 1.6$\times$10$^4$ M$_\odot$. This independent constraint from integrated light complements previous limits based on resolved-star counts and strengthens the case for Cloud-9 as a candidate starless galaxy.

AI.tldr: Ultra-deep GTC/HiPERCAM imaging fails to detect any stellar light from the dark galaxy candidate Cloud-9, reaching surface-brightness limits of ~31 mag/arcsec^2 and setting an upper limit on total stellar mass of 1.6×10^4 M_sun, strengthening its classification as a candidate starless galaxy.
AI.motivation: To independently constrain the stellar content of the dark galaxy candidate Cloud-9 using integrated light, complementing previous limits from resolved-star counts and testing whether it truly lacks stars.
AI.method: Ultra-deep imaging with HiPERCAM at the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC), reaching surface-brightness limits of 31.4 and 31.0 mag/arcsec^2 in g and r bands (~10x deeper than previous imaging). The stellar limits were interpreted assuming an old, metal-poor stellar population.
AI.result: No stellar emission detected within the central 1'×1' (~1.3×1.3 kpc) region. This yields an upper limit on stellar surface mass density of ~0.01 M_sun/pc^2 and total stellar mass ≤1.6×10^4 M_sun.
AI.conclusion: The independent integrated-light constraint agrees with resolved-star count limits and strengthens the case for Cloud-9 as a candidate starless (dark) galaxy.

title: Gas-phase and Surface Chemistry in the Massive Star-Forming Region RCW\,120
summary: We analysed broadband emission spectra of a dense molecular clump in RCW 120, obtained with the APEX telescope in the 200--260 GHz range, in order to investigate molecular formation pathways in regions of massive star formation at an early evolutionary stage. We examined the correlations between the molecular column densities derived under the LTE assumption. An excess of methanol was found in the southern part of the dense clump relative to its northern part, while the abundances of other molecules, such as CH$_3$CN and CH$_3$CCH, remain comparable. The methanol abundance is also elevated relative to that of other oxygen-bearing molecules, such as OCS and SO. To identify possible causes of the enhanced methanol abundance in the southern part of the clump, we carried out simulations with the astrochemical model Presta in a two-phase approximation, accounting for chemical processes both in the gas phase and in the mantles of dust grains. The modelling shows that the enhanced gas-phase methanol abundance may be due to photodesorption from icy mantles. At Av values between $4^{m}$ and $6^{m}$, methanol desorbs efficiently from the ice mantles of dust grains upon interaction with photons, but is not yet destroyed by UV radiation in the gas phase. A strong linear correlation between molecular column densities indicates that the molecules form in the same phase --- either in the gas phase or on dust. Their integrated intensity maps may nevertheless differ, as is the case for CCH and CH$_3$CN. If two molecules form in different phases --- one in the gas phase and the other in dust mantles --- no correlation is observed, as for CCH and CH$_3$OH. The weak correlation between methanol and the oxygen-bearing molecules that form on dust suggests that only the upper part of the dust mantles, rich in CO ice, is destroyed in the southern part of the clump.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes APEX broadband emission spectra (200-260 GHz) of a dense molecular clump in RCW 120 to investigate molecular formation pathways in early massive star formation. LTE column density correlations reveal elevated methanol abundance in the southern clump, attributed by Presta astrochemical simulations to photodesorption from icy grain mantles at Av ≈ 4-6 magnitudes. Strong column density correlations indicate same-phase molecular formation, while weak methanol-oxygen-bearing molecule correlations suggest only the CO-rich upper mantle is destroyed in the south.
AI.motivation: To understand molecular formation pathways in massive star-forming regions at early evolutionary stages by analyzing broadband emission spectra of a dense clump in RCW 120, particularly investigating why methanol is anomalously enhanced in the southern part of the clump compared to other molecules.
AI.method: The authors used the APEX telescope to obtain broadband spectra (200-260 GHz) of the dense clump, derived LTE molecular column densities, examined correlations between molecular abundances, and performed astrochemical simulations with the Presta model in a two-phase approximation (gas phase + dust grain mantles) to test chemical pathways.
AI.result: Methanol shows excess abundance in the southern clump relative to the north, while CH3CN and CH3CCH remain comparable. The Presta model indicates enhanced gas-phase methanol arises from photodesorption off icy mantles at Av between 4-6 magnitudes, where photodesorption operates but UV destruction in gas phase is not yet effective. Strong linear correlations indicate same-phase formation (e.g., CCH and CH3CN both gas-phase), while no correlation between different-phase molecules (e.g., CCH and CH3OH). Weak methanol-oxygen-bearing dust-formed molecule correlations suggest only the CO-ice-rich upper mantle is destroyed in the south.
AI.conclusion: The enhanced southern methanol abundance is best explained by photodesorption from dust ice mantles at moderate extinction. Molecular column density correlations can be used to infer whether molecules form in the same phase (gas or dust), and differing integrated intensity maps reflect distinct formation sites. The selective destruction of only the upper CO-ice-dominated mantle layer in the south explains the weak correlations between methanol and other dust-formed oxygen-bearing molecules.

title: A comparative study of emergent dark energy models
comment: 22 pages, 15 figures, accepted for publication in the Physics of the Dark Universe journal
summary: Late (emergent) dark energy models that involve a hyperbolic tangent in their dynamic equations have achieved success due to their simplicity, the possibility of resolving the Hubble tension, and, in some cases their consistency with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) results. Among the most studied are the Phenomenological and General Emergent Dark Energy Models (PEDE and GEDE, respectively), the variable curvature model, and the graduated dark energy model. Our goal is to include the curvature term in the models and perform a robust comparative study using diverse data samples, in particular, Cosmic Chronometers, Type Ia supernovae, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations from DESI-DR1, and Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation. This study presents the Universe age, the deceleration, the $w_{eff}$ parameter reconstruction, the redshift transition, and the best fit for the free parameters of each model. Our collected evidence from Akaike Information Criterion and Bayesian Information Criterion indicates that the best candidate is the PEDE model. Nevertheless, the variable-curvature model is the only model that exhibits a decelerated phase near $z=0$, consistent with the results from DESI.

AI.tldr: The paper compares late (emergent) dark energy models with hyperbolic tangent dynamics—PEDE, GEDE, variable curvature, and graduated dark energy—against multiple cosmological datasets (Cosmic Chronometers, Type Ia supernovae, DESI-DR1 BAO, and CMB). Statistical criteria favor PEDE as the best overall candidate, but the variable-curvature model uniquely exhibits a decelerated phase near z=0, consistent with DESI results.
AI.motivation: Emergent dark energy models using hyperbolic tangent functions have shown promise in resolving the Hubble tension and aligning with DESI observations, but a robust comparative study incorporating curvature and multiple data samples is needed to determine which model best describes cosmological observations.
AI.method: The authors incorporate curvature terms into four emergent dark energy models (PEDE, GEDE, variable-curvature, and graduated dark energy) and perform a comparative Bayesian analysis using diverse datasets: Cosmic Chronometers, Type Ia supernovae, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations from DESI-DR1, and Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation. Model comparison is conducted using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), alongside reconstruction of Universe age, deceleration parameter, effective equation-of-state (w_eff), and transition redshift.
AI.result: The AIC and BIC evidence indicate that the PEDE model is the best-fitting candidate overall. However, the variable-curvature model is the only model that predicts a decelerated phase near z=0, which is consistent with DESI results. The study also provides best-fit free parameters, Universe age, deceleration, w_eff reconstruction, and transition redshift for each model.
AI.conclusion: The PEDE model is statistically preferred among the emergent dark energy models considered, yet the variable-curvature model stands out as the only one reproducing the DESI-consistent decelerated phase near z=0, suggesting model-dependent behaviors warrant further investigation.

title: The superclumps of the local Milky Way. Supercloud fragmentation and the sites of star formation
summary: Using a Gaia-based 3D dust map of the solar neighborhood, we analyze the internal structure of the seven local superclouds. We identify quasi-periodic density enhancements along their spines, which we term "superclumps" and show that 73% of the known star-forming regions in the dust map volume can be associated with them. Across the six superclouds with more than one recovered superclump, the spacings are characteristic per cloud: $\sim$150-250 pc for the Split, Malpolon Cloud and Vela Ridge Cloud, and $\sim$250-380 pc for the Radcliffe Wave, Natrix Cloud and Sagittarius Spur Extension. The observed separations are two to three times smaller than the $\sim$560 pc predicted for an isolated self-gravitating cylinder of the same effective diameter, indicating fragmentation under external pressure rather than in isolation. The recurring spacing suggests that giant molecular cloud assembly is not a local, stochastic process, but is instead influenced by the large-scale gravitational fragmentation of the parent superclouds. Regardless of the precise formation mechanism, the superclumps occupy a critical intermediate scale in the hierarchical organization of the interstellar medium, bridging the gap between the kiloparsec-scale gas lanes and the $\sim$10-100 pc scale of individual giant molecular clouds.

AI.tldr: Using a Gaia-based 3D dust map, the authors identify quasi-periodic density enhancements ("superclumps") along the spines of seven local superclouds. 73% of known star-forming regions are associated with these superclumps, whose characteristic spacings (150-250 pc or 250-380 pc) are two to three times smaller than predicted for isolated self-gravitating cylinders, indicating fragmentation under external pressure. Superclumps occupy a critical intermediate scale in interstellar medium hierarchy, bridging kiloparsec-scale gas lanes and 10-100 pc giant molecular clouds.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal structure of local superclouds and determine whether giant molecular cloud assembly follows large-scale gravitational fragmentation or a local, stochastic process.
AI.method: Analyzes a Gaia-based 3D dust map of the solar neighborhood to identify density enhancements along supercloud spines, measures their characteristic spacings, and compares observed separations with predictions from isolated self-gravitating cylinder models.
AI.result: Seven local superclouds show quasi-periodic superclumps; 73% of star-forming regions associate with them. Spacings are 150-250 pc or 250-380 pc depending on the cloud, two to three times smaller than the ~560 pc prediction for isolated self-gravitating cylinders, indicating external-pressure-driven fragmentation.
AI.conclusion: Superclumps represent a critical intermediate scale in the hierarchical organization of the interstellar medium, bridging kiloparsec-scale gas lanes and individual giant molecular clouds, implying large-scale gravitational fragmentation controls molecular cloud assembly rather than local stochastic processes.

title: On what scales does strong lensing robustly constrain the mass profile of low-mass perturbers?
summary: Galaxy-galaxy strong gravitational lensing is an established method to detect and characterise low-mass haloes, which are otherwise too faint to be directly observed. Recent analyses have shown empirically that there exists a characteristic radius within which the projected enclosed mass of these haloes can be robustly measured. Here we provide a physically and mathematically motivated definition of this robust radius based on the Fisher information matrix. We show that for any spherically symmetric smooth profile with at least two free parameters, there exists a pivot radius at which estimates of the projected mass become decorrelated from the local logarithmic slope and have minimum relative uncertainty. As a result, the projected mass within this radius can be recovered consistently by any profile that fits the data well enough. This robust radius coincides, to leading order, with the weighted geometric mean of the arc pixel distances from the halo, where the weights depend on the perturber deflection angle, the macro-model magnification, and the source surface brightness gradient. Beyond leading order, corrections are of order the weighted log-width of the arc. The data constraining power on the local properties of the halo profile beyond amplitude is shown to depend on the radial leverage of the arc around the perturber, and on the imprint of the perturber deflection angle on high signal-to-noise-ratio pixels. Our definition generalises to both subhaloes and line-of-sight haloes and naturally captures the important physical aspects of the problem and the effect of the data resolution and signal-to-noise ratio.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a physically and mathematically motivated definition of the "robust radius" in galaxy-galaxy strong lensing—a characteristic radius within which projected enclosed mass of low-mass haloes can be reliably measured—derived from Fisher information matrix analysis.
AI.motivation: Galaxy-galaxy strong gravitational lensing is an established method to detect and characterise low-mass haloes that are too faint for direct observation. Recent empirical analyses have shown there exists a characteristic radius within which the projected enclosed mass of these haloes can be robustly measured, but a rigorous physical/mathematical foundation for this radius was lacking.
AI.method: Using the Fisher information matrix, the authors prove that for any spherically symmetric smooth profile with at least two free parameters, there exists a pivot radius at which estimates of projected mass become decorrelated from the local logarithmic slope and have minimum relative uncertainty. They derive that this robust radius coincides, to leading order, with the weighted geometric mean of arc pixel distances from the halo, with weights depending on perturber deflection angle, macro-model magnification, and source surface brightness gradient. Beyond leading order, corrections scale as the weighted log-width of the arc.
AI.result: The projected mass within the robust radius can be recovered consistently by any profile that fits the data sufficiently well. The constraining power on local halo profile properties beyond amplitude depends on the radial leverage of the arc around the perturber and the imprint of the perturber deflection angle on high-SNR pixels. The definition generalises to both subhaloes and line-of-sight haloes, and captures data resolution and signal-to-noise effects.
AI.conclusion: The robust radius provides a rigorous, first-principles foundation for mass measurements in strong lensing, naturally generalising to both subhaloes and line-of-sight haloes while capturing the essential physics and practical data effects.

title: The GASKAP-HI Survey towards the Magellanic Clouds: Cold Atomic Gas Survival and Evolution in the Large Magellanic Cloud
comment: 36 pages, 20 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We use atomic hydrogen (HI) absorption detections from the GASKAP-HI survey to investigate the properties of cold atomic gas in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Using the radiative transfer method, we decompose 155 sightlines into 330 cold neutral medium (CNM), 2 thermally unstable neutral medium (UNM), and 310 warm neutral medium (WNM) components. We find that the CNM in the LMC exhibits higher optical depths (median 0.46), lower spin temperatures (median $\sim$37 K), broader linewidths (median $\sim$4.9 km s$^{-1}$), and slightly lower CNM fractions (median $\sim$23%) than in the Milky Way. We examine the connection between the CNM, molecular gas, and star formation, finding that CNM correlates more closely with molecular gas than WNM, while molecular gas shows a tighter relation with star formation. Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) formation begins near $N{_\mathrm{HI,CNM}}\sim10^{20}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$, and nearly all sightlines with $N_{\mathrm{HI,CNM}}>10^{21}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ contain molecular gas. The CNM fraction increases with visual extinction ($A_V$), and the LMC maintains CNM fractions comparable to those in the Milky Way at substantially lower $A_V$, likely due to higher local densities and a longer line-of-sight depth. Sightlines near expanding shells tend to show higher CNM fractions, although this is partly driven by higher total HI column densities. Finally, the CNM kinematics generally follow the HI disk rotation, with about 7% of components showing velocity offsets greater than $25~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$, likely tracing inflows or outflows driven by stellar feedback or large-scale interactions within the Magellanic System.

AI.tldr: Using GASKAP-HI survey data, the authors decompose 155 sightlines in the LMC into CNM, UNM, and WNM components via radiative transfer. The LMC's CNM shows higher optical depths, lower spin temperatures, broader linewidths, and slightly lower CNM fractions than the Milky Way. CNM correlates more closely with molecular gas than WNM, H2 formation begins near N_HI,CNM ~ 10^20 cm^-2, and CNM fractions increase with visual extinction. About 7% of components show velocity offsets >25 km/s, likely tracing feedback-driven flows.
AI.motivation: To characterize the properties of cold atomic gas (CNM) in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and understand its relationship with molecular gas and star formation, providing insight into how the cold neutral medium behaves in a low-metallicity, dwarf galaxy environment compared to the Milky Way.
AI.method: HI absorption detections from the GASKAP-HI survey are analyzed using the radiative transfer method to decompose 155 sightlines into 330 CNM, 2 UNM, and 310 WNM components. Properties such as optical depth, spin temperature, linewidth, and CNM fraction are measured and compared with the Milky Way. Correlations with molecular gas, star formation, visual extinction, and kinematic offsets are examined.
AI.result: The LMC CNM has a median optical depth of 0.46, spin temperature ~37 K, linewidth ~4.9 km/s, and CNM fraction ~23%, differing from Milky Way values. CNM correlates more strongly with molecular gas than WNM, H2 formation starts near N_HI,CNM ~ 10^20 cm^-2, and sightlines with N_HI,CNM > 10^21 cm^-2 nearly all contain molecular gas. CNM fraction increases with A_V but reaches Milky Way-equivalent values at lower A_V. Expanding shells show higher CNM fractions partly due to higher column densities. ~7% of components exhibit velocity offsets >25 km/s, likely indicating feedback-driven inflows/outflows.
AI.conclusion: The LMC's cold neutral medium differs in key physical properties from the Milky Way's, reflecting its lower metallicity and different environment. The CNM is tightly linked to molecular gas formation and star formation, and the galaxy maintains comparable CNM fractions at lower extinction due to higher densities and longer path lengths. Kinematic signatures suggest active gas flows from stellar feedback and Magellanic System interactions.

title: One-point matter PDFs beyond TopHat filters
summary: We study the one-point probability distribution function (PDF) for matter densities averaged with an arbitrary spherically symmetric window function. The PDF is analytically modeled within the path integral framework, enabling a non-perturbative description of large-scale structure. It contains a leading order contribution controlled by the spherically symmetric gravitational collapse dynamics, as well as an order-one factor arising from aspherical fluctuations. We develop a numerical pipeline to compute the leading spherical-collapse part of the PDF and apply it to a family of window functions interpolating between the TopHat and Gaussian filters in coordinate space, as well as to a window function with non-monotonic radial dependence. We find that the PDF weakly depends on the choice of the filter, provided the width of the filter is normalized to yield a fixed linear averaged density variance. For each filter and each value of the averaged density, our pipeline gives the most probable density profile. We find that these profiles vastly differ for different filters in the case of overdensities, but closely follow a universal curve at underdensities. We obtain a perturbative expression for the aspherical part of the PDF valid at small density contrasts. We find from it that all PDFs are equally sensitive to the effective field theory (EFT) corrections accounting for short-scale clustering, regardless of how smooth the filter's boundary is. We test our PDF model against the results of high-resolution N-body simulations. The agreement is excellent for filters with widths larger than 10 Mpc/h. Small discrepancies at a few percent level arise for narrower filters and are interpreted as higher-order perturbative corrections.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an analytical model for the one-point probability distribution function (PDF) of matter densities averaged with arbitrary spherically symmetric window functions within a path integral framework. The PDF, consisting of a spherical-collapse leading term and an order-one aspherical fluctuation factor, is computed numerically across various filters. The PDF weakly depends on the filter choice when widths are normalized to fixed variance; most probable density profiles differ for overdensities but are universal for underdensities; effective field theory corrections are equally important regardless of filter smoothness. The model agrees excellently with N-body simulations for filters wider than 10 Mpc/h.
AI.motivation: To provide a non-perturbative, analytical description of the large-scale structure matter density PDF that works for arbitrary spherically symmetric window functions, going beyond the standard TopHat and Gaussian filters and enabling robust comparisons with simulations.
AI.method: The PDF is modeled analytically within the path integral framework, separating a leading-order spherical-collapse contribution from an order-one aspherical fluctuation factor. A numerical pipeline computes the spherical-collapse part for a family of window functions interpolating between TopHat and Gaussian in coordinate space, plus a non-monotonic radial filter. A perturbative expression for the aspherical part at small density contrasts is obtained, including EFT corrections for short-scale clustering.
AI.result: The PDF weakly depends on filter choice once the window width is normalized to fixed linear density variance. Most probable density profiles differ significantly across filters for overdensities but follow a universal curve for underdensities. All PDFs are equally sensitive to EFT corrections regardless of filter boundary smoothness. Agreement with high-resolution N-body simulations is excellent for filters wider than 10 Mpc/h, with only few-percent discrepancies for narrower filters attributed to higher-order perturbative corrections.
AI.conclusion: The path-integral-based PDF model robustly describes matter density statistics for arbitrary spherically symmetric window functions, with weak filter dependence after variance normalization and strong agreement with simulations for sufficiently large filter widths.

title: The curious case of HCO$^+$: Extreme abundances under extreme conditions
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 13 pages, 16 figures
summary: Context. HCO$^+$ is widely observed in both Galactic and extragalactic environments and typically exhibits abundances of $10^{-9}-10^{-8}$. However, recent modeling studies suggest that in environments exposed to elevated cosmic-ray ionization rates and strong thermal or mechanical processing its abundance may increase by several orders of magnitude. Aims. To interpret these predictions, we need to understand the physical conditions that produce extreme HCO$^+$ abundances and the chemical pathways that drive these enhancements. Methods. We used UCLCHEM, a gas-grain chemical code, to model the chemistry of HCO$^+$ in dense molecular, protostellar, and shocked gas under elevated cosmic-ray ionization rates ($ζ\ge 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$). Results. Extreme HCO$^+$ enhancements leading to $X$(HCO$^+$) $\gtrsim 10^{-4}$ occur only under specific combinations of temperature, density, and cosmic-ray ionization rate, primarily in protostellar and shocked gas. Increasing density generally suppresses the peak HCO$^+$ abundance, requiring higher ionization rates to produce comparable enhancements. More importantly, the extreme enhancements seem to be very dependent on the chemical network used (in our case UMIST12 versus UMIST22, with the latter leading to extreme abundances). These differences among networks arise from the removal of the destruction pathway of HCO$^+$: C + HCO$^+$ $\rightarrow$ CO + CH$^+$, and propagate to several other species including N$_2$H$^+$, H$_2$O, and H$_3$O$^{+}$.

AI.tldr: The paper models HCO+ chemistry using UCLCHEM across dense molecular, protostellar, and shocked gas under elevated cosmic-ray ionization rates, finding that extreme HCO+ abundances (~10^-4) occur only under specific conditions and depend critically on the chemical network used, specifically whether the destruction pathway C + HCO+ → CO + CH+ is included.
AI.motivation: HCO+ is commonly observed with abundances of 10^-9 to 10^-8, but modeling suggests it could be enhanced by orders of magnitude in environments with elevated cosmic-ray ionization rates and strong thermal/mechanical processing. The authors aim to understand which physical conditions produce these extreme HCO+ abundances and what chemical pathways drive them.
AI.method: The study employs UCLCHEM, a gas-grain chemical code, to model HCO+ chemistry in dense molecular, protostellar, and shocked gas under elevated cosmic-ray ionization rates (ζ ≥ 10^-15 s^-1). The models are run with different chemical networks (UMIST12 vs UMIST22) to assess network dependence.
AI.result: Extreme HCO+ enhancements (X(HCO+) ≥ 10^-4) occur only under specific combinations of temperature, density, and cosmic-ray ionization rate, mainly in protostellar and shocked gas. Higher density suppresses peak HCO+ abundance. Critically, extreme enhancements are strongly network-dependent: they appear with UMIST22 but not UMIST12, due to the removal of the C + HCO+ → CO + CH+ destruction pathway in the newer network. These differences propagate to other species including N2H+, H2O, and H3O+.
AI.conclusion: Extreme HCO+ abundances are highly sensitive to both physical conditions (temperature, density, cosmic-ray ionization rate) and chemical network choices. The absence of the C + HCO+ destruction channel in UMIST22 leads to order-of-magnitude enhancements that may not be physically robust, highlighting the need for careful benchmarking of chemical networks when interpreting observations of high HCO+ abundances.

title: Probing cosmological phase transitions with SKAO through nano-Hz gravitational-wave portal
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Pasechnik01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: The recent evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background at nano-Hz frequencies from pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) provides a strong science case for exploring cosmological histories and phase transitions at the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO). The latter cosmological events are of primary interest for physics of the early Universe associated with out-of-equilibrium and relaxation phenomena in the vicinity the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) epoch as well as those originating from dark sectors or other phenomena beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. Such a novel GW portal provides a complimentary access to particle physics phenomena that have so far escaped detection at particle colliders, and also probes fundamental aspects of out-of-equilibrium dynamics beyond the perturbation theory and their cosmological implications. This chapter aims at elucidating most interesting physics cases, theoretical models and approaches, as well as cosmological scenarios that are of particular relevance for future GW measurements at SKAO. We elaborate on how such measurements can deepen our understanding of particle interactions and violent processes in the early Universe, and discuss possible competitive advantages and complementarity of SKAO in this research compared to other experiments.

AI.tldr: This chapter explores how the stochastic gravitational wave background detected by pulsar timing arrays at nano-Hz frequencies provides a new window into cosmological phase transitions and early-Universe physics—particularly around the QCD epoch and beyond the Standard Model scenarios—and discusses how the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO) can uniquely probe these phenomena, complementing particle colliders and other GW experiments.
AI.motivation: Recent PTA detection of a stochastic GW background at nano-Hz frequencies opens a new observational channel to study cosmological histories, phase transitions, and out-of-equilibrium dynamics in the early Universe that have escaped detection at particle colliders.
AI.method: The chapter reviews theoretical models, physics cases, and cosmological scenarios for early-Universe phase transitions (QCD epoch, dark sectors, beyond-Standard-Model physics), and evaluates the capabilities, advantages, and complementarity of SKAO for future nano-Hz gravitational wave measurements.
AI.result: SKAO is positioned as a powerful and complementary facility for probing cosmological gravitational wave signatures, offering access to particle physics phenomena beyond collider reach and out-of-equilibrium dynamics beyond perturbative approaches, working alongside other experiments.
AI.conclusion: The gravitational wave portal at nano-Hz frequencies, combined with SKAO's observational capabilities, can significantly deepen our understanding of particle interactions and violent early-Universe processes, with clear scientific advantages and complementarity relative to other experimental facilities.

title: Angular momentum in isolated disc galaxies: Insights from TNG100
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures and 1 table. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Angular momentum is a fundamental property that shapes the evolution of disc galaxies, strongly influencing the internal mechanisms that regulate star formation. Its content within disc galaxies is predicted to change over time, mainly as a result of external processes that regulate galaxy evolution. While several numerical studies paint a complex picture of angular momentum variation with environmental mechanisms, a recent observational finding suggests that galaxies are subject to angular momentum loss when they undergo interactions. By studying the stellar angular momentum of simulated disc galaxies selected at various degrees of isolation, we aim to investigate whether isolation affects the stellar angular momentum content of disc galaxies and assess whether the environmental trends previously reported for baryonic angular momentum may also be reflected exclusively in the stellar component. We selected star-forming disc galaxies in the IllustrisTNG simulation suite, for which we computed an isolation parameter based on local density. Using a density threshold, we identified isolated discs from non-isolated galaxies and performed a comparative study of their angular momentum content against other evolutionary parameters. We find that isolation alone does not define the angular momentum content of a galaxy. Rather, whether a disc is gas-rich or gas-poor is directly linked to the specific angular momentum content, $j_*$, of its stellar disc.

AI.tldr: Using the IllustrisTNG simulation suite, the authors investigate whether galactic isolation affects the stellar specific angular momentum content of disc galaxies. They find that isolation alone does not determine stellar angular momentum; instead, whether a disc is gas-rich or gas-poor is directly linked to its stellar specific angular momentum ($j_*$).
AI.motivation: Angular momentum is fundamental to disc galaxy evolution and star formation regulation, yet its variation with environmental mechanisms remains complex. A recent observational finding suggests galaxies lose angular momentum during interactions, motivating a numerical study to test whether isolation affects stellar angular momentum content and whether environmental trends seen in baryonic angular momentum also appear in the stellar component alone.
AI.method: The authors select star-forming disc galaxies from the IllustrisTNG simulation suite. They compute an isolation parameter based on local density and, using a density threshold, separate isolated discs from non-isolated galaxies. They then perform a comparative analysis of angular momentum content, isolating the stellar component ($j_*$), against other evolutionary parameters.
AI.result: Isolation alone does not define the angular momentum content of a galaxy. Rather, the gas-rich vs. gas-poor nature of a disc is directly linked to the specific stellar angular momentum content, $j_*$.
AI.conclusion: Environmental isolation is not the primary driver of stellar angular momentum content in disc galaxies; instead, gas content plays a more direct role in determining the stellar specific angular momentum. This suggests the previously reported environmental trends in baryonic angular momentum may not be mirrored in the stellar component exclusively.

title: Physical Calibration of a Minimal Effective Field Theory of the Three-Dimensional Lyman-$α$ Forest
summary: We study a minimal effective field theory description of the three-dimensional Lyman-$α$ forest using the Sherwood and Sherwood--Relics hydrodynamical simulations. We model the Lyman-$α$ flux auto-power spectrum and its cross-correlation power spectrum with the dark matter density field using a tree-level bias model supplemented by the leading counterterms and stochastic contributions. We find that the model describes the simulated auto- and cross-power spectra well up to $k_{\mathrm{max}}=3\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ and $k_{\mathrm{max}}=2\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, respectively. We analyse simulations spanning multiple redshifts, reionisation histories, box sizes and resolutions to assess the robustness of the model. Even within this minimal model, we find strong parameter degeneracies, highlighting the need for independent constraints on nuisance parameters in applications to real data analyses. The redshift evolution of the linear bias parameters is consistent with previous simulation-based studies and is driven primarily by the evolution of the effective optical depth, $τ_{\mathrm{eff}}$. We also find that the inferred parameters are affected by the resolution of the simulation and, to a lesser extent, by the simulation box size. We also explore the impact of reionisation history, finding that variations mainly affect the linear bias parameters over the range of scales considered. Moreover, we find empirical correlations between model parameters and the Lyman-$α$ forest density bias that show some scatter, indicating that one single parameter is not enough to determine the model parameters. Finally, we compare our results with theoretical predictions from analytical models of the Lyman-$α$ forest.

AI.tldr: This paper tests a minimal effective field theory (EFT) bias model for the 3D Lyman-α forest using Sherwood and Sherwood-Relics hydrodynamic simulations, finding it describes auto- and cross-power spectra up to k_max=3 and 2 h Mpc⁻¹ respectively, while revealing parameter degeneracies, simulation resolution effects, and reionization-history impacts.
AI.motivation: To assess whether a minimal EFT-based bias model can reliably describe the Lyman-α forest power spectra from simulations, and to evaluate its robustness to variations in redshift, reionization history, box size, and resolution, informing its applicability to real data analyses.
AI.method: The authors model the Lyman-α flux auto-power spectrum and its cross-correlation with the dark matter density field using a tree-level bias model with leading counterterms and stochastic contributions, fitted against Sherwood and Sherwood-Relics hydrodynamic simulations spanning multiple redshifts, reionization histories, box sizes, and resolutions.
AI.result: The model works well up to k_max=3 h Mpc⁻¹ (auto-spectrum) and 2 h Mpc⁻¹ (cross-spectrum). Strong parameter degeneracies are found, requiring independent nuisance constraints. Bias parameter redshift evolution is consistent with prior studies and driven by effective optical depth. Parameters are affected by simulation resolution and, to a lesser extent, box size. Reionization history variations mainly affect linear bias parameters. Empirical correlations with density bias show scatter, indicating one parameter is insufficient. Results are compared with analytical model predictions.
AI.conclusion: A minimal EFT bias model can reproduce simulated Lyman-α forest power spectra on relevant scales, but care is needed due to parameter degeneracies and systematics from simulation resolution, box size, and reionization history; independent constraints on nuisance parameters are essential for real-data applications.

title: The [Ne V] AGN Diagnostic in SDSS-IV/eBOSS: An Anticorrelation Between Ionization State and AGN Luminosity in Low-Redshift Coronal-Line Galaxies
comment: 23 pages, 16 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to The Open Journal of Astrophysics. For the eBOSS-DAP catalog and associated data products, see https://datalab.noirlab.edu/data/sdss#sdss-iv-eboss-dap-value-added-catalog ; for the eBOSS-DAP source code, see https://github.com/owenmatthewsa/ebossdap
summary: Traditional narrow-line diagnostics fail at high redshift, where low metallicity drives star-forming galaxies and Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) into overlapping regions of the Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (BPT) diagram. Coronal lines, with ionization potentials exceeding 100 eV, offer a robust alternative: they cannot be produced by normal stellar populations, arise almost exclusively from AGN or fast shocks, and are insensitive to abundance evolution. Among these, the [Ne V] doublet is the brightest optical coronal line tracer of AGN activity. Existing coronal line catalogs contain only about 1750 objects, too few to statistically assess the completeness and purity of [Ne V]-selected AGN samples. We identify 33,817 galaxies with [Ne V] S/N > 5 at z = 0.147-1.12 in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV extended Baryon Oscillations Spectroscopic Survey (SDSS-IV/eBOSS), exceeding the combined literature total by more than an order of magnitude. [Ne V] preferentially selects rapidly accreting, relatively unobscured AGN; only 41.5% of BPT AGN show detectable emission. By stacking spectra that lack [Ne V] on a grid of black hole mass and [O III] luminosity, we recover [Ne V] in the majority of bins, implying that non-detections reflect limited survey sensitivity rather than a deficit of coronal emission. We find [Ne V]/[Ne III] is only weakly correlated with [O III]/[O II]. Galaxies with high [Ne V]/[Ne III] for their [O III]/[O II] ratio have lower Eddington ratios and are more likely classified as LIERs or Composites. The [Ne V]/[O III] ratio shows a strong anticorrelation with [O III] luminosity, with the most extreme coronal-line strengths found among the lowest-luminosity AGN, in analogy with the accretion states of stellar-mass black holes. Comparison with a sample of z=2-9 [Ne V]-detected galaxies suggests some, but not all, high-redshift AGN follow the same relations.

AI.tldr: The authors present a large catalog of 33,817 [Ne V]-selected AGN at z=0.147-1.12 from SDSS-IV/eBOSS, more than an order of magnitude beyond previous literature. They find [Ne V] preferentially selects rapidly accreting, relatively unobscured AGN, recover [Ne V] in stacked spectra of non-detections, and report new correlations between coronal-line ratios and AGN properties, including an analogy between the [Ne V]/[O III] versus [O III] luminosity anticorrelation and stellar-mass black hole accretion states.
AI.motivation: Traditional narrow-line diagnostics (e.g., BPT diagram) fail at high redshift because low metallicity causes star-forming galaxies and AGN to overlap. Coronal lines like [Ne V] offer a robust alternative, but existing catalogs contain only ~1,750 objects—too few for statistical assessment of completeness and purity of [Ne V]-selected AGN samples.
AI.method: The authors identify galaxies with [Ne V] S/N > 5 at z=0.147-1.12 in SDSS-IV/eBOSS. They analyze detection statistics relative to BPT AGN, stack spectra lacking [Ne V] as a function of black hole mass and [O III] luminosity to test sensitivity limits, and examine correlations between coronal-line ratios ([Ne V]/[Ne III], [Ne V]/[O III]) and AGN properties such as Eddington ratio and ionization classification.
AI.result: The sample includes 33,817 [Ne V]-detected galaxies. Only 41.5% of BPT AGN show detectable [Ne V]. Stacking recovers [Ne V] in most mass/luminosity bins, indicating non-detections are largely sensitivity-limited. [Ne V]/[Ne III] weakly correlates with [O III]/[O II]; high coronal ratios correlate with lower Eddington ratios and LIER/Composite classification. [Ne V]/[O III] strongly anticorrelates with [O III] luminosity, with extreme coronal strengths in low-luminosity AGN. High-redshift (z=2-9) [Ne V] galaxies partially follow the same relations.
AI.conclusion: This study provides an order-of-magnitude larger coronal-line AGN sample than previously available, demonstrating that [Ne V] is an effective high-redshift AGN tracer. The results establish quantitative relations between coronal-line strengths and AGN physical properties, and suggest a connection to stellar-mass black-hole accretion-state phenomenology, though not all high-redshift AGN follow the same scaling relations.

title: Model independent lensing sub-structure detection with multiply-imaged star clusters constellations
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures (+3 extra figures in the appendix)
summary: A broad class of dark matter (DM) models predicts the existence of sub-structures residing in DM haloes on sub-resolvable angular scales. Techniques to extract such a generic feature from diffraction-limited observations are lacking. In this work, we propose a model-independent 'super-resolving' method applicable to strong gravitational lens systems that is fully data-driven, without reference to any lens models. This method relies on a specific way of applying the optical Liouville theorem across multiple scales in the imaging data, a technique we refer to as geometrical-duality. We test this method using realistic simulations and apply it to a 'constellation' consists of 11 compact star clusters seen in two giant arcs in the lensing cluster SMACS0723 imaged by JWST as a proof-of-concept. We find reasonable self-consistency with the expectation of non-detection given the statistical sensitivity, except for one pair of star clusters. Such an outlier can be explained in the context of CDM as sub-haloes lensing in the mass range $M_{\rm sub} = 10^8 - 10^9\,M_\odot$, for which the corresponding Einstein radius is smaller than the diffraction limit of JWST.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-independent, data-driven "super-resolving" method for detecting dark matter sub-structures in strong gravitational lens systems by applying the optical Liouville theorem across scales (geometrical-duality). Tested on realistic simulations and applied to 11 compact star clusters in two giant arcs of SMACS0723 (JWST data), it finds reasonable self-consistency with non-detection expectations except for one pair of star clusters, which could be explained by CDM sub-haloes of mass 10^8–10^9 M⊙ with Einstein radii below JWST's diffraction limit.
AI.motivation: A broad class of dark matter models predicts sub-structures in DM haloes on sub-resolvable angular scales, but no generic, model-independent technique exists to extract this signal from diffraction-limited observations.
AI.method: The method is a fully data-driven "super-resolving" approach for strong gravitational lens systems that applies the optical Liouville theorem across multiple imaging scales (termed "geometrical-duality"), requiring no reference to lens models.
AI.result: The method was validated on realistic simulations and applied to 11 compact star clusters in two giant arcs of SMACS0723 from JWST. All pairs showed self-consistency with non-detection within statistical sensitivity, except one outlier pair that can be explained as sub-halo lensing in the mass range M_sub = 10^8–10^9 M⊙, whose Einstein radii are smaller than JWST's diffraction limit.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometrical-duality super-resolving technique enables model-independent detection of dark matter sub-structures below the diffraction limit in strong lens systems, demonstrated as a proof-of-concept on JWST data of SMACS0723, with one candidate outlier consistent with CDM sub-halo predictions.

title: The Random Magnetic Field of the Milky Way
summary: We constrain the large-scale isotropic random component of the Galactic magnetic field using the Planck reconstruction of the 408 MHz synchrotron sky. Our analysis simultaneously fits the random-field structure, the synchrotron contributions of the coherent field and local foregrounds, and isotropic and dipolar offsets. A new element of the analysis is the use of excess polarized emission at 30 GHz to model local foregrounds, allowing us to retain 97% of the sky without absorbing these structures into Galaxy-wide features of the magnetic field. Across variations in the coherent-field model, cosmic-ray electron distribution, sky mask, and field profile, we consistently find that the dominant random-field component is a vertically compact disk with a local rms strength of about 4 $μ$G and a 1/e scale height of approximately 1 kpc, substantially thinner than in most previous models. An annular enhancement in the inner Galaxy improves the fit to the data, whereas we find no evidence for either a large-scale spiral pattern or a thick random-field disk. The fits also yield an intensity monopole of 4-7 K, whose possible origin we discuss. We quantify the implications of the inferred random field for the angular smearing of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays. Compared with previous models, the sky-median smearing angle is smaller by up to a factor of 1.7, and by up to 2.4 in individual directions.

AI.tldr: The paper constrains the large-scale random component of the Galactic magnetic field using Planck's reconstruction of the 408 MHz synchrotron sky, finding a vertically compact disk with ~4 μG local rms strength and ~1 kpc scale height, thinner than previous models, with implications for ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray deflection.
AI.motivation: To better constrain the previously poorly-understood random component of the Galactic magnetic field, which is crucial for modeling cosmic ray propagation and interpreting synchrotron observations.
AI.method: Simultaneous fitting of random-field structure, coherent-field synchrotron contributions, local foregrounds (modeled via excess polarized emission at 30 GHz), and isotropic/dipolar offsets against Planck's 408 MHz synchrotron sky reconstruction. Various coherent-field models, cosmic-ray electron distributions, sky masks, and field profiles are tested.
AI.result: The dominant random-field component is a vertically compact disk with ~4 μG local rms strength and ~1 kpc 1/e scale height, substantially thinner than most previous models. An annular enhancement in the inner Galaxy improves fit; no evidence for large-scale spiral pattern or thick random-field disk was found. An intensity monopole of 4-7 K was also derived. Sky-median cosmic ray smearing angle is up to 1.7x smaller and up to 2.4x smaller in individual directions compared to previous models.
AI.conclusion: The random Galactic magnetic field is much more vertically compact than previously assumed, which significantly alters predictions for ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray angular smearing; the improved foreground modeling enables retaining 97% of the sky in the analysis.

title: Diversity of Galaxy Centers from Small-Scale Isocurvature
summary: The observed diversity of galaxy centers motivates the possibility that the local dark matter composition may vary among galaxies. In conventional multicomponent dark matter scenarios, however, large stochastic variations in the relative abundances are not generically expected, with the cold component typically remaining dominant. We perform $N$-body simulations with a subdominant ultralight dark matter component carrying significant large-amplitude small-scale isocurvature perturbations. We find that although nonlinear evolution largely homogenizes its fraction on galactic scales,ultralight dark matter can still be enhanced and even dominate the centers of small halos because large initial ultralight dark matter fluctuations seed early potential wells that later form halo centers. The ultralight-dominated region can extend beyond $0.01R_{\rm vir}$ and account for more than half of the central dark matter density, even for a cosmological ultralight dark matter fraction below $O(10\%)$. This central segregation provides a possible route to stochastic cusp--core diversity, potentially explaining the observed diversity of galaxy centers.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how a subdominant ultralight dark matter (ULDM) component with large-amplitude small-scale isocurvature perturbations can become enhanced and even dominate the centers of small halos, leading to stochastic cusp-core diversity in galaxy centers.
AI.motivation: The observed diversity of galaxy centers suggests local dark matter composition may vary among galaxies, but conventional multicomponent dark matter scenarios do not generically predict large stochastic variations in relative abundances, with the cold component typically remaining dominant.
AI.method: N-body simulations with a subdominant ultralight dark matter component carrying large-amplitude small-scale isocurvature perturbations.
AI.result: Nonlinear evolution largely homogenizes the ULDM fraction on galactic scales, but ULDM can still be enhanced and even dominate the centers of small halos because large initial ULDM fluctuations seed early potential wells that later form halo centers. The ULDM-dominated region can extend beyond 0.01R_vir and account for more than half of the central dark matter density, even for a cosmological ULDM fraction below O(10%).
AI.conclusion: The central segregation of ULDM provides a possible route to stochastic cusp-core diversity, potentially explaining the observed diversity of galaxy centers.

title: High-Energy Neutrino Constraints on memory burdened Bardeen and Kerr Primordial Black Holes
summary: The quantum memory burden effect can suppress the late-time Hawking evaporation of primordial black holes (PBHs), allowing PBHs below the standard evaporation threshold of approximately $10^{15}\,\mathrm{g}$ to survive until the present epoch and potentially contribute to the dark matter abundance. We investigate primary and secondary neutrino emission from memory burdened Bardeen and Kerr PBHs, including Galactic and extragalactic fluxes and the effects of memory suppression, Bardeen regularization, and Kerr rotation. We constrain their abundance using observations from IceCube, Super-Kamiokande, and ANTARES, together with the projected sensitivities of IceCube-Gen2, GRAND200k, and Hyper-Kamiokande. We find that Bardeen regularization and Kerr rotation produce qualitatively different effects. Increasing the Bardeen parameter suppresses the Hawking temperature and neutrino flux, thereby weakening the abundance constraints. In contrast, rapidly rotating Kerr PBHs that retain a significant residual spin at the onset of the memory burdened phase can exhibit enhanced neutrino emission and substantially stronger constraints. Increasing the memory burden suppression index $k$ reduces the flux normalization but also allows lighter and hotter PBHs to survive, shifting the relevant signal toward higher energies. Consequently, HESE provides the leading sensitivity for weak suppression, whereas IceCube-Gen2 and GRAND200k become particularly important for stronger suppression. These results demonstrate the complementarity of current and future neutrino observations in probing memory burdened PBHs and the effects of regular geometry and rotation on their evaporation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates neutrino emission from memory burdened Bardeen and Kerr primordial black holes (PBHs), which can survive to the present epoch due to the quantum memory burden effect suppressing Hawking evaporation. Using Galactic and extragalactic neutrino fluxes, the authors constrain PBH abundance with current (IceCube, Super-Kamiokande, ANTARES) and future (IceCube-Gen2, GRAND200k, Hyper-Kamiokande) observatories, finding that Bardeen regularization suppresses the flux while rapid Kerr rotation enhances it, with the leading sensitivity depending on the memory burden suppression index.
AI.motivation: The memory burden effect allows PBHs below the standard evaporation threshold (~1e15 g) to survive until today and potentially constitute dark matter. Understanding the signature of such PBHs through neutrino emission is essential for probing their abundance and distinguishing the effects of black hole geometry (Bardeen vs. Kerr) and rotation on evaporation.
AI.method: The authors compute primary and secondary neutrino fluxes from memory burdened Bardeen and Kerr PBHs, accounting for Galactic and extragalactic contributions, memory suppression, Bardeen regularization, and Kerr rotation. They then derive abundance constraints using data from IceCube, Super-Kamiokande, and ANTARES, and project sensitivities for IceCube-Gen2, GRAND200k, and Hyper-Kamiokande.
AI.result: Bardeen regularization suppresses the Hawking temperature and neutrino flux, weakening constraints, while rapidly rotating Kerr PBHs with residual spin exhibit enhanced neutrino emission and much stronger constraints. Increasing the memory burden suppression index k reduces flux normalization but allows lighter, hotter PBHs to survive, shifting signals to higher energies. HESE gives leading sensitivity for weak suppression, whereas IceCube-Gen2 and GRAND200k are most important for strong suppression.
AI.conclusion: Current and future neutrino observatories demonstrate complementary sensitivity in probing memory burdened PBHs, revealing the important roles of regular black hole geometry and rotation in shaping PBH evaporation and dark matter abundance constraints.
